I would like to add my 2 cents, although I'm not big on taking advice, so I don't expect others to be big on taking mine. What worked for me, when I kicked the junkie life, was to look at what the life was producing, in me and others around me. It was total destruction, devastation, loss, and depression. I worked to correlate the drug in my mind with its effects, until I successfully made myself see drugs as DISGUSTING, repulsive, the last thing in the world I'd want. I also worked to look forward, instead of backward. Instead of thinking about how I was an addict and a mess and how much I was into that drug, etc, I let go of that identity and thoughts, and just started looking forward to what I would become and what I wanted for myself in the future. I also found new sources of satisfactions and interests, like running(aerobic exercise is so beautiful and satisfying: a rich, wonderful array of endogenous, healthy, balanced substances), and I made nutrition very important.

Today, I am 100% a different human being and no longer identify even 1% with what I used to be. It's almost like I never was that, now. I learned important lessons, for moving forward, from it, but it has no part in me today, and that's exactly how I want it to be. I'm happier now, by magnitudes, than I ever was back then. And if you ever fall, pick yourself right back up, don't blame yourself, and move forward again.

Do you know how you get stronger? You push your muscles enough that microscopic tears start to form throughout that muscle, and then, while you're resting, your body reforms the muscle along the tears in a way that can perform even better than it did before the muscle was torn. If you don't use a muscle for several months/years, then it will degrade over time, to the point that it might fail entirely the next time you try to use it (which is why nurses make sure to help coma patients go through various stretches to keep their muscles semi-active).

In a lot of ways, the human mind performs in the same way: If you don't use it, you can lose all of your mental connections to the outside world (such as by becoming a psychopath or falling into a degenerate lifestyle, like you see very often among modern Marxists). However, if you can recognize your problem before you've fallen to the very bottom, you can recover and emerge from the darkness even stronger than when you first fell in (or at least have more mental resolve about staying on the right path).

Life isn't just about the destination, it's about the journey. There is a reason why humanity loves to hear about their heroes stumbling into darkness before emerging with their ideals largely intact: it is something that everyone can relate to, in one way or another, and it helps us recognize that, as imperfect human beings, it is okay for us to fall, so long as we try our best to get back up and keep moving forward.
